cim: NPEs and the Computerization of Everything That Moves
cim_eredeti: NPEs and the Computerization of Everything That Moves
szoveg_eredeti:
[Updated and Expanded from As Vehicles Become Computerized, NPE Patent Owners Are Targeting Automakers (2021)]

In 2021, we published As Vehicles Become Computerized, NPE Patent Owners Are Targeting Automakers, an article examining how non-practicing entities (NPEs) were increasingly targeting the automotive sector as vehicles became computers on wheels. The thesis was straightforward: as automakers adopted the same software, connectivity, and sensor technologies that had long defined high-tech products, they would face the same patent assertion campaigns that software and electronics companies had been defending against for years.

That prediction proved correct. But the story did not stop at the vehicle. Today, the same software-defined, connected, and data-rich technology layers that attracted NPE attention to automotive products are being deployed across an expanding range of physical systems: commercial drones, warehouse robots, autonomous delivery vehicles, surgical and industrial robotics, agricultural automation, defense platforms, and other physical AI systems. The connected car was not an endpoint; it was the first wave of a broader transformation.

This article is part of a twelve-week series on autonomous systems, physical AI, and patent strategy. In prior articles, we established an expanded taxonomy of patentable inventions across the physical AI landscape, presented a comprehensive IP strategy playbook for autonomous systems companies, examined the data on whether patent filings help physical AI companies raise capital, analyzed what acquirers now diligence in AI and autonomy deals, and examined where competitor-driven physical AI patent disputes are likely to emerge. Here, we turn to the defensive side of the equation: how NPEs and patent assertion entities (PAEs) identify targets, what the current litigation data reveals, and what companies building physical AI products should do to prepare.

The core observation is this: the NPE risk that first followed the connected car is now following the connected machine. Any company whose product depends on wireless communications, GPS or geolocation, sensor data, cloud connectivity, remote monitoring, user interfaces, or software-based device control should consider patent assertion risk as part of its IP strategy, product development process, and investor readiness.

The 2021 article began with a simple observation: automakers, high-tech software companies, and electronics companies were increasingly facing similar challenges as vehicles became computers on wheels. Software and electronics companies were historically among the largest targets of patent infringement lawsuits brought by NPEs. As vehicles incorporated more software, more connectivity, and more electronic components, the automotive sector began to look like the technology sector from a patent assertion perspective.

The data at the time was striking. According to RPX Corp.’s Q3 2021 report, NPEs had their busiest third quarter since 2016, adding 595 defendants to litigation. Of thirteen tracked industry sectors, the automotive sector experienced the largest percentage increase in NPE-targeted defendants from Q3 2020 to Q3 2021, rising 182% (from 11 defendants to 31). That single data point illustrated a broader trend: as vehicles became more connected and software-defined, NPEs recognized that patents originally asserted against smartphones, networking equipment, and e-commerce platforms could be asserted against automotive products as well.

The specific NPE campaigns identified in 2021 targeted technology features that were, by then, standard in modern vehicles:

The pattern was not random. Each of these technology areas, including GPS, cellular, infotainment, and USB connectivity, had been the subject of extensive patent prosecution and NPE litigation in the smartphone and consumer electronics sectors for years before NPEs turned to automotive targets. Once a critical mass of vehicles incorporated the same features, the automotive sector became a new source of licensing and litigation revenue for patent assertion campaigns.

The 2021 article concluded that, although the automotive industry might prefer to avoid patent wars while the electric and autonomous vehicle market was still developing, NPEs appeared to have a different agenda and were poised to apply their assets and experience to the automotive sector. That conclusion has proven accurate, and the assertion risk has since expanded far beyond automobiles.

Since the publication of the 2021 article, NPE activity has not only continued but accelerated. Several developments in the patent litigation landscape are relevant to any company operating in the autonomous systems and physical AI space.

According to RPX, U.S. patent litigation increased substantially in 2024, with NPE filings climbing 21.6% and operating-company filings rising 16.8%. Unified Patents reported in its 2025 Year in Review that NPE district court filings jumped an additional 21.6% in 2025 compared with 2024, and that overall district court patent case filings increased 12% year over year. NPEs filed 55.4% of all district court patent cases in 2025, a majority of all patent litigation nationwide.

The high-tech sector bore the heaviest concentration. According to Unified Patents, NPEs were responsible for 90.3% of all high-tech patent litigation in 2025, a disproportionate share even against the 55.4% NPE filing rate across all sectors. Unified defines high-tech as software, hardware, and networking technologies, all of which overlap directly with the technology layers used in autonomous systems and physical AI products. Any company whose product incorporates software-based control, networked communications, sensor processing, or cloud connectivity falls squarely within the zone of technologies most frequently targeted by NPE litigation.

Venue selection continues to play a central role in NPE litigation strategy. Unified Patents reported that the Eastern District of Texas and the Western District of Texas together accounted for more than 60% of NPE litigation filings in 2025. For defendants, this concentration has practical implications: companies operating nationally or globally should expect that NPE complaints may be filed in Texas regardless of the defendant’s principal place of business, and should evaluate venue-transfer strategies early in the litigation timeline.

Inter partes review (IPR) at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has long been a cornerstone of NPE defense strategy. Under 35 U.S.C. § 311, a non-owner may petition for inter partes review on grounds of anticipation (§ 102) or obviousness (§ 103) based on patents or printed publications. The institution standard under § 314 requires a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner will prevail on at least one challenged claim, and institution decisions are final and nonappealable.

However, PTAB procedural dynamics shifted materially in 2025. Unified Patents reported that PTAB procedural denials rose sharply, with a record-high 607 denials issued in 2025. The institution rate against NPE-owned patents fell from 64.6% in Q1 2025 to just 33.6% in Q4 2025, a steep decline that significantly changes the calculus for defendants relying on IPR as their primary defense mechanism.

At the same time, requests for ex parte reexamination reached an all-time high of 726 in 2025, suggesting that some defendants and practitioners are exploring alternative post-grant proceedings in response to increased PTAB discretionary denials.

Strategic takeaway: Defendants should no longer assume that IPR will be the central path for challenging the validity of asserted patents.
